docs.title: The Researcher as Orchestrator
docs.text:
The researcher as orchestrator is the organizing idea of this book: instead of performing every task personally, the researcher directs a team of agents, sets direction, supplies domain judgment, resolves conflicts among them, and decides what is true. The model developed in later chapters assigns roughly 20 planning agents, which explore, decompose, and specify, and 10 execution agents, which write code, run analyses, and prepare figures. The numbers are a design target, not a law; they express the idea that planning is cheap to parallelize and execution needs closer supervision.

In the running example, the orchestrator's day might look like this. Several planning agents each take a different part of the ADC comparison: one surveys architectures, one drafts the measurement procedure (S1), one proposes how to estimate uncertainty. You read their outputs, resolve a disagreement between two of them about record length by reasoning from the converter's bandwidth, and approve the procedure. Execution agents then run the simulations (S2), compute simulated ENOB (S4), and, when the chips are measured, the measured ENOB (S5). You are not typing the scripts. You are choosing what gets run, checking what comes back against the test oracle from the coding section, and signing the result. The work has not become easier so much as it has moved: from production to direction and verification.

The orchestrator's scarcest resource is attention, not typing speed. Each additional agent adds output to review, so the useful size of a team is set by how much you can verify, not by how many agents you can launch. Chapters 9 and 10 develop roles, handoffs, and the supervision techniques that keep a team of this kind honest.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Research in electrical engineering is a workflow of repeatable tasks with checkable outputs, and AI systems now absorb a substantial share of the procedural layer. The researcher's job is to supply what the workflow cannot: the question, the domain judgment, and the accountability.

The main points to carry forward:

  • The workflow consists of five everyday tasks (literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, manuscript preparation) chained into a pipeline whose trustworthiness is bounded by its weakest stage.
  • A precise research question with a metric and a threshold is the cheapest quality control available when using AI.
  • Generative AI, large language models, assistants, and agents form a chain; an agent adds tools and a loop to an assistant, and with them, actions you did not individually approve.
  • LLM output is a hypothesis until checked, because fluent text can be false.
  • Productivity must include verification time, and reproducibility now includes recording prompts, models, and settings.
  • Task decomposition into subtasks with checkable outputs is what makes delegation safe.
  • Human review belongs where an action is irreversible, leaves your control, or becomes a reported result.
  • The researcher as orchestrator directs and verifies; accountability for the science stays with you.

You Have the Map

You can now name the five research tasks, tell an assistant from an agent by who closes the loop, and decide where a human review point belongs. That is the vocabulary and the habit of checking that the rest of this book builds on.

The next chapter looks inside the models themselves, so that the failure modes introduced here, hallucination in particular, become something you can reason about rather than something that surprises you. Round up the evidence, and bring the question you would most like an agent to help with.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter explains the mechanics a researcher needs to know about large language models: how text becomes tokens, how context windows limit long tasks, and how prompts and completions work. It covers training data, knowledge cutoffs, and the causes of hallucination and fabricated citations. After this chapter you can explain why a fluent answer may still be wrong and choose an interface for your work.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator

A Model You Can Reason About

A tool you cannot predict is a tool you cannot supervise. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at a wrong answer and say which mechanism produced it, and to budget a long task before it silently fails. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: What You Send and What Comes Back
docs.text:
Every interaction with a language model reduces to the same exchange: text goes in, and text comes out. The text that goes in is the prompt. The text that comes out is the completion. These two words carry more weight than they appear to, because every technique in the remaining chapters of this book is a way of controlling one or the other.

The most common mistake about the prompt is to equate it with what you typed. The prompt is everything the model receives for this one response: any instructions the application inserted before your message, the earlier turns of the conversation, any files or pasted documents, the output of tools the model called, and finally your latest message. The model has no memory of previous conversations beyond what is present in this assembled text. When a chat application appears to remember what you said ten minutes ago, it is because it sent the earlier turns again as part of the new prompt.

The completion is the text the model generates in response. It is produced one piece at a time, each piece chosen on the basis of the prompt and the pieces already produced, until the model emits a special stop signal or reaches a configured length limit. To see what "generated, not retrieved" means in practice, imagine sending the prompt "A SAR ADC resolves one bit per" twice. One run might continue "comparison cycle" and another "clock period", both reasonable and both different. Neither is looked up; each is the continuation the model judged likely at that moment. Two consequences follow, and both matter for research use. First, the completion is generated, not retrieved: nothing is looked up in a store of facts, and the same prompt can yield different completions on different runs. Second, the model has no separate channel for "what I am sure of". Confident and uncertain statements are produced by the same mechanism, which is why a completion cannot be trusted by its tone.

It helps to see the whole exchange once as structured data. Most programmatic interfaces represent a prompt as a list of messages. In the example below, role says who is speaking (system for standing instructions from the application or developer, user for you, assistant for earlier model replies), content is the text itself, and max_tokens caps the length of the completion. The field names follow a common convention; they differ slightly between providers.

{
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system",
     "content": "You are a careful assistant for analog circuit research. Say 'unknown' rather than guess."},
    {"role": "user",
     "content": "Define ENOB in one sentence."},
    {"role": "assistant",
     "content": "ENOB is the resolution of an ideal converter that would add the same noise and distortion as the real one."},
    {"role": "user",
     "content": "Now give the formula that relates it to SINAD."}
  ],
  "max_tokens": 200
}

Everything in that list, together, is the prompt for the next completion. The model's answer to the last message is conditioned on the first three, and the model sees them again from the beginning on every turn.

The Model Only Has What Is Sent

Think of each response as a new reader who has been handed a folder and told to continue it. If a fact is not in the folder, it is not in the room. When an answer ignores something you said earlier, ask first whether it was still in the folder.

docs.title: Tokens and Tokenization
docs.text:
Models do not read characters or words. They read tokens, the units into which text is divided before the model sees it. A token is often a whole common word, but it may be a fragment of a word, a single character, a run of whitespace, or a piece of punctuation. Tokenization is the procedure that converts a string into its sequence of tokens, and it is fixed for a given model family: the same string tokenizes the same way each time, but different models may split it differently.

Tokens matter to a researcher for three practical reasons. They are the unit in which providers bill (usage is priced per token, and output tokens are commonly priced higher than input tokens). They are the unit in which the model's capacity is measured, because the context window described below is a count of tokens. And they explain odd failures: a model that handles a word as three fragments has no direct view of its letters, which is why character-level tasks such as counting the letters in a word are more error-prone than they look.

The following illustrative split shows the idea. The string is 39 characters long. The tokenization is invented for this chapter to show typical behavior, and a real tokenizer would divide it differently; each | marks a token boundary.

The| SAR| ADC| reached| 9|.|6| EN|OB| at| 1| MS|/s|.

That is 14 tokens for roughly eight words. Notice that common words such as "The" and "reached" are single tokens, while a number is split into digits and a decimal point, and an acronym that is rare in everyday text is split into fragments. This is the general pattern for technical writing: equations, code, part numbers, units, and acronyms cost more tokens per word than ordinary prose.

A commonly used rule of thumb for English prose is about four characters per token, or about three-quarters of a word per token. For planning, divide a word count by 0.75 to estimate tokens: a paper of 8,250 words is about 11,000 tokens. Treat this as an estimate to within perhaps twenty percent for prose and as an under-estimate for equation-heavy or code-heavy text. When the number matters, count with the provider's own tokenizer or the usage figures the API returns.

Estimate Before You Paste

Words divided by 0.75 gives a usable token estimate for prose. Multiply by 1.3 if the document is mostly equations or code. If the estimate lands within a quarter of your limit, count it properly before you rely on it.

docs.title: The Context Window
docs.text:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can take into account at once, counting both the prompt and the completion. It is the single most important structural limit on what a model can do in one pass. A context limit is the specific numeric value of that maximum for a particular model, and exceeding it has one of three outcomes depending on the application: the request is rejected with an error, the oldest content is dropped, or the completion is cut off partway through a sentence. The second outcome is the dangerous one, because nothing looks wrong. The model simply continues without the instructions or documents that fell off the front.

The window is a shared budget, and the completion draws from the same pool as the prompt. The arithmetic is simple:

\[ \text{tokens available for completion} = \text{window} - \left( t_{\text{system}} + t_{\text{history}} + t_{\text{attachments}} + t_{\text{message}} \right) \]

Here \( t_{\text{system}} \) is the tokens of standing instructions, \( t_{\text{history}} \) is the earlier turns, \( t_{\text{attachments}} \) is any pasted or attached documents, and \( t_{\text{message}} \) is your latest message. If the right-hand side is negative, the prompt alone does not fit.

A worked example, with illustrative numbers, shows how quickly a window fills. Suppose a model has a 32,000-token window. A standing instruction of 600 tokens, a conversation history of 4,000 tokens, a pasted paper of 8,250 words (about 11,000 tokens), and a question of 400 tokens add up to 16,000 tokens, leaving 16,000 for the completion. That is comfortable. Now you paste a second paper of the same length. The prompt becomes 27,000 tokens, only 5,000 remain, and a request for a 6,000-token literature summary cannot be completed in full. The step that went wrong was not the second paste but not doing the subtraction first.

Window sizes differ enormously between models, from tens of thousands to well over a million tokens, and they change with each model release, so look up the current figure in the provider's documentation rather than relying on a number in a book. Two caveats hold regardless of size. A larger window costs more to fill, because you pay for every input token. And a model does not use all positions in a long context equally well: material in the middle of a very long prompt is more often overlooked than material at the start or end, so a document that fits is not a document that was read with equal care.

The first MicroSim lets you practice the subtraction. Before you use it, make sure the term attachment is clear: an attachment here means any document whose text is placed into the prompt, whether pasted or uploaded.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and types the tokens remaining.
  2. The learner chooses "fits" or "does not fit" for the requested completion and submits both answers together.
  3. The sim shows the worked subtraction from the "Why" column and the stacked bar for that challenge.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses a 32,000-token window, a 600-token system prompt, a 4,000-token history, a paper of 8,250 words (about 11,000 tokens), and a 400-token question, leaving 16,000 tokens. A second paper leaves 5,000 tokens, which cannot hold a 6,000-token completion. The chapter states that tokens are about words divided by 0.75.

Truncation Rarely Announces Itself

A common trap is a long session in which the first instructions quietly fall off the window and the model drifts from your constraints. It happens because many chat tools drop the oldest content instead of failing. Restate the constraints near the end of the prompt, or start a fresh session with a short summary of the decisions so far.

docs.title: System Prompts
docs.text:
A system prompt is a block of standing instructions placed at the start of every prompt, before the conversation. In a chat product it is written by the application's developer and is normally hidden from the user. In your own scripts and agents you write it yourself. It sets the model's role, tone, constraints, and format, and it persists across turns because the application resends it each time.

Two properties make it useful and one makes it risky. It is cheap leverage: a single paragraph stating the discipline you want ("cite only documents provided; answer 'unknown' if the documents do not contain the answer") changes every later response. It is also not a security boundary: the model treats system text and user text as input to the same process, and sufficiently insistent or adversarial text elsewhere in the prompt can override it. Chapter 4 returns to this under prompt injection. Finally, a system prompt consumes context on every turn, so a 3,000-token standing prompt on a 32,000-token window costs about a tenth of your budget before you have said anything.

docs.title: Temperature and Sampling
docs.text:
At each step the model computes a score for every token in its vocabulary and converts the scores into probabilities. Temperature is a setting that reshapes those probabilities before one token is chosen. Low temperature sharpens the distribution toward the highest-scoring token, so output is more repeatable. High temperature flattens it, so lower-scoring tokens are chosen more often and output varies more. If \( z_i \) is the score of token \( i \) and \( T \) is the temperature, then

\[ p_i = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j / T}}. \]

With three candidate tokens scoring 2.0, 1.0, and 0.0, temperature 1.0 gives probabilities of 66.5%, 24.5%, and 9.0%. Lowering the temperature to 0.5 gives 86.7%, 11.7%, and 1.6%, and raising it to 2.0 gives 50.6%, 30.7%, and 18.6%. The ranking never changes, only the odds. For extraction, reformatting, and code, prefer low temperature. For brainstorming alternatives, a higher setting is a feature. Low temperature does not make a model more correct; it makes a wrong answer more repeatable.

docs.title: Training Data and the Knowledge Cutoff
docs.text:
A model's behavior comes from its training data, the large body of text, code, and other material it was fitted to. During training, the model's parameters are adjusted so that it predicts the continuation of its training text better. This stage is followed by additional tuning on curated instruction-and-response examples and on human preference judgments, which is what makes a raw text predictor behave like an assistant. You do not need the optimization details for this course. You need to know what the process implies for what the model can and cannot reliably do.

First, a model's knowledge is a compressed statistical summary of text, not a database. Frequent, widely repeated, well-documented material is represented well. Rare, recent, proprietary, or highly specialized material is represented poorly or not at all. In electrical engineering this gradient is easy to see: a model will explain a two-stage Miller-compensated op-amp or the Nyquist criterion fluently, because that material is saturated in textbooks and lecture notes. It will be far shakier about the exact performance table of a 2024 conference paper, the quirks of a vendor's undocumented model-card parameter, or your group's internal test fixture, which it has never seen.

Second, the training data bounds what kinds of mistakes are natural. A model reproduces patterns in its data, including errors, outdated practice, and the biases of who wrote what is online. A SPICE netlist idiom that was common in older forum posts may be reproduced even where a newer syntax is recommended.

Third, the data has an end date. The knowledge cutoff is the date after which the model has seen essentially no training data. Anything published or changed after that date is unknown to the model unless you supply it in the prompt or let a tool fetch it. The cutoff is earlier than the model's release date, often by many months, and it is not a sharp line: coverage of the last months before the cutoff is thin. For a researcher the consequence is practical. Ask a model for "the state of the art" in a fast-moving topic such as a new memory technology or a new standard, and it will describe the field as of its cutoff with no indication that time has passed.

Question type Training data helps? What to do Textbook concept (Nyquist sampling, KCL) Yes, strongly Use directly, then spot-check a formula Established method with many tutorials Yes Use as a draft; verify the exact equation Result from a specific recent paper Poorly Supply the paper's text or look it up Your own data, code, or measurements No Put it in the prompt Events or releases after the cutoff No Supply the information or use a search tool

Table 1. When training data can and cannot be relied on.

docs.title: Hallucination and Fabricated Citations
docs.text:
A hallucination is output that is fluent and confident but not grounded in the prompt or in fact. The word is imperfect, since it suggests a malfunction, whereas the behavior is the model working as designed. Its objective is to produce a plausible continuation. When the true answer is well represented in its training data, the plausible continuation and the true one coincide. When it is not, the model still produces the most plausible-looking text, and plausibility without truth is exactly what a hallucination is.

Hallucination tends to occur under identifiable conditions, and the list below is worth keeping in view when you decide how much to trust a completion:

  • The request asks for specifics the model cannot have: exact numbers, page numbers, part numbers, dates.
  • The topic is rare, recent, or after the knowledge cutoff.
  • The prompt presupposes something false ("Explain why the Foo-Smith theorem implies...").
  • The task requires exact multi-step computation done in the model's head rather than with a tool.
  • The prompt has pushed the model to always produce an answer and gave it no sanctioned way to say "unknown".

A fabricated citation is the signature hallucination of research use: a reference with plausible authors, a plausible title, a real-sounding venue and year, and often a correctly formatted DOI, for a paper that does not exist or that says something different from what is attributed to it. It arises for the same reason as any hallucination. A citation has a highly regular structure, and the model can generate a well-formed instance of that structure about a topic without any lookup. Fabricated citations are dangerous precisely because they are well formed: they pass a glance.

Citations fail in four distinct ways, and the distinction is what a verification procedure must detect:

  1. Fabricated: no such paper exists.
  2. Wrong details: the paper exists, but year, venue, volume, pages, or an author is wrong.
  3. Unsupported claim: the paper exists and the details are right, but it does not say what the model claimed.
  4. Verified: the paper exists, the details match, and the paper supports the claim.

Checking requires leaving the model. Resolve the DOI, search the exact title in a bibliographic database, compare authors, venue, and year with what the database shows, and open the paper to confirm the sentence it is cited for. The same discipline applies when the model is correct; it is simply cheap to do once and expensive to skip once.

Asking the Model to Double-Check Is Not Checking

A tempting shortcut is to ask the same model, "Are these citations real?" The model will answer fluently, and the answer is generated by the same mechanism that produced the citations. Use the model to format a reference list, not to certify it. Certify with a database lookup you ran yourself.

A worked example. A model, asked for prior work on calibration of SAR ADCs, returns "Lindqvist and Okafor (2019), Charge-Redistribution SAR ADC Calibration Using Sparse Foreground Estimation, IEEE JSSC, 54(7)." The record is invented here for illustration. You search the exact title in two bibliographic databases and find nothing. You search the authors and find no joint work. The venue and volume exist, which is why the citation looked right. The verdict is fabricated, and the useful move is to discard it and ask for search terms instead, then run those terms in the database.

The second MicroSim lets you practice the four-way classification on records that are invented for the exercise.

docs.title: Choosing the Model: Size, Reasoning, Modality, and Benchmarks
docs.text:
Model size is the number of trainable parameters in a model, the adjustable numbers fitted during training, usually stated in billions. Within a model family, larger models are generally more capable on difficult tasks, and also slower and more expensive to run. Size is a rough guide, not a ranking. Training data quality, tuning, and design differ between families, so a well-tuned smaller model can outperform a larger one on a given task, and many hosted models do not disclose their size at all. For a researcher the practical rule is to match the model to the task: a small, fast model is adequate for reformatting a bibliography or classifying abstracts, and a larger model is worth its cost for ambiguous derivations.

A reasoning model is a model trained or configured to generate an extended sequence of intermediate steps, sometimes hidden from the user, before it gives a final answer. This tends to improve results on multi-step problems such as derivations, debugging, and planning. The trade-off is that the intermediate steps are tokens too: they count against the context window, they add latency, and they are usually billed. Use a reasoning model where the task is hard and the answer is checkable, and do not pay for it on a task that a short, direct answer already handles.

A multimodal model accepts, and sometimes produces, more than text: images, audio, or documents with layout. For electrical engineering the useful case is giving the model a schematic screenshot, an oscilloscope capture, a waveform plot, or a datasheet page. Reading qualitative structure from an image (what topology is this, which trace is the clock) is often good. Reading numeric values off a plot or tracing a dense schematic is unreliable, and these are exactly the readings that feed conclusions, so extract values from the source data when you have them.

A model benchmark is a standardized set of tasks with a scoring rule, used to compare models. Published benchmark scores are useful for a first screening and poor predictors for your task, because the benchmark may not resemble your work, models may have seen the test items during training, and a single aggregate score hides the failure types you care about. The reliable response is to build a small benchmark of your own: ten to twenty tasks from your own research with answers you have already verified, run against each candidate model. Chapter 7 develops this idea into skill testing, and Chapter 17 into verification.

Property What it buys What it costs Use it when Larger model size Better on hard, ambiguous tasks Latency, price The task is difficult and quality matters more than speed Reasoning model Better multi-step accuracy Extra tokens, latency, price The answer is checkable and the steps are many Multimodal input Works on figures and pages Reading of values is unreliable You need structure, not exact numbers Public benchmark score Fast first screening May not predict your task Narrowing a long list of candidates

Table 2. The properties of Section "Choosing the Model" and when to reach for each.

docs.title: Chat Interfaces and the Command Line
docs.text:
There are two ways you will mostly reach a model, and the difference between them determines what kind of work each supports.

A chat interface is a conversational application, in a browser or a desktop or phone app, in which you type messages and read replies. It is the lowest-friction way to start, and it is well suited to exploring an idea, drafting, asking for an explanation, or examining a single document. Its limits follow from its design. The conversation lives in the application, so it is hard to reproduce exactly. Files must be uploaded by hand. Actions are limited to what the application permits. And the settings that affect output, such as the model version, are often not visible in the transcript.

A command line interface (CLI) is a text interface in a terminal where you type commands and run programs, and a CLI-based AI tool runs the model from that environment. The difference is not stylistic. A tool in the terminal can read and write files in your project, run your scripts, call other command-line programs, and be invoked from a shell script, a makefile, or a scheduled job. Tools such as Claude Code and Codex CLI work this way. Because the whole interaction is text in files and shell history, it can be version-controlled, repeated, and inspected, which is the property reproducible research requires.

A minimal non-interactive use illustrates the point. The command below is a generic form: ai-cli is a placeholder for whichever tool you use, --prompt supplies the instruction, cat sends a file into the tool's input, and > writes the reply to a file. Flag names differ between tools.

# Generic form: send a results file and an instruction, save the reply for review
cat results/enob_sweep.csv | ai-cli --prompt "List any row where ENOB falls by more than 0.5 bit relative to the previous row. Output one line per row: row number, old ENOB, new ENOB." > review/enob_flags.md

Three things are worth noticing. The input file, the prompt, and the output file are all named, so the step can be rerun and compared. The prompt states an output format, which makes the result easy to check. And nothing in the command gives the tool permission to modify your data, which is the right default. Chapter 8 develops what happens when a CLI agent is given permission to write files and run code.

Dimension Chat interface Command line interface Typical use Exploration, drafting, explanation Repeatable tasks, file and code work Access to your files Manual upload Direct, subject to permission Reproducibility Low: the transcript lives in the app High: commands and files are in your repository Automation Not possible Scriptable and schedulable Setup cost Almost none Install, authenticate, learn the commands Risk surface Limited to what you paste Includes file changes and shell commands

Table 3. Chat interface versus command line interface.

A reasonable path for most researchers is to begin in a chat interface to build intuition, move to the command line when a task recurs or touches files, and keep every command-line invocation in the project's version history.

The Terminal Is a Skill, Not a Gate

If the command line feels slower than the chat window at first, that is normal; typing a command costs more than clicking. You already run simulators and scripts from a shell. Start with one recurring task, such as the flagging command above, and let the saved command do the work the second time.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
A language model turns a prompt into a completion one token at a time, and everything it uses must be present in that prompt. Its reliability is a property of its training data, which is broad but not authoritative and ends at a cutoff date. Plausibility, not truth, is what it optimizes, so fluent output of any kind has to be verified against something outside the model.

The main points to carry forward:

  • The prompt is everything sent, including system instructions, history, files, and tool output, and the completion is generated, not retrieved.
  • Tokens are the unit of billing and capacity, and technical text costs more tokens per word than prose.
  • The context window is a shared budget for prompt and completion, and overflow may be silent.
  • A system prompt sets standing behavior, uses budget on every turn, and is not a security boundary.
  • Temperature reshapes the odds without changing the ranking, and low temperature does not make output more correct.
  • Training data and a knowledge cutoff bound what the model can know, so supply recent, rare, and private material yourself.
  • Hallucinations, including fabricated citations, are the model working as designed. Verify with a lookup you run.
  • Size, reasoning, modality, and benchmarks are trade-offs to match to a task, and your own small benchmark beats a public score.
  • Chat interfaces suit exploration and command lines suit repeatable, file-touching, reproducible work.

You Can Read the Mechanism

You can now budget a context window, say what temperature does and does not change, and sort a citation into verified, wrong-detail, unsupported, or fabricated. Those are the checks that stand between a fluent answer and a true one.

The next chapter turns this knowledge into decisions: which model, through which access path, at what cost, and how to write a prompt that states its output format. Round up the evidence, and bring one task you would like to hand to a model.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Research Workflows and the Researcher as Orchestrator
  • Chapter 2: How Language Models Work

From Using a Model to Choosing One

This chapter is where you stop asking "what can the model do?" and start asking "which model, reached how, at what price, and told what?" By the end you will be able to choose a model for a task and write a prompt precise enough that you can check the answer. Trust, but verify!

docs.title: Reaching a Model Through an API
docs.text:
In Chapter 2 you met two ways of using a model: a chat interface and a command line. Both sit on top of a third thing that you need to understand to choose well. API access is the ability to send a prompt to a model from a program, over the network, and receive the completion as data. API is short for application programming interface. A chat product is, in effect, a graphical program that makes these calls for you.

The distinction matters because an API call is repeatable and scriptable. You send a request that names the model, supplies the messages, and sets parameters such as the temperature and the maximum number of output tokens. You receive a response that includes the completion and a count of the tokens used. You authenticate with a secret API key that identifies your account and is tied to your billing. Treat the key like a password: store it in an environment variable or a secrets manager, never inside a prompt, a notebook that you share, or a repository. A key committed to a public repository is typically scraped within minutes.

An API gives you three things a chat window does not. You can run the same prompt over a hundred inputs in a loop. You can pin the exact model version and settings and write them in your lab notebook. And you can wire the model into a pipeline, so that its output is checked by a script before a human sees it. Each of these is a prerequisite for the verification practices in later chapters.

An API also brings three practical constraints, each of which can break a pipeline that worked on five inputs and fails on five thousand.

  • Token cost is the price of a request, computed from the number of tokens in and out.
  • Latency is the time between sending a request and receiving the response.
  • A rate limit is the maximum number of requests, or tokens, a provider will accept from you in a time window.

Token cost is the product of usage and price. Providers quote prices per million tokens, with different prices for input tokens and output tokens. If \( t_{\text{in}} \) and \( t_{\text{out}} \) are the input and output token counts and \( p_{\text{in}} \) and \( p_{\text{out}} \) are the prices per million tokens, then

\[ C = \frac{t_{\text{in}}\, p_{\text{in}} + t_{\text{out}}\, p_{\text{out}}}{10^{6}}. \]

Consider a worked example with illustrative prices: 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 dollars per million output tokens. You want to classify 200 abstracts. Each request carries about 500 input tokens, a 400-token abstract plus a 100-token instruction, and returns about 150 output tokens. The totals are 100,000 input tokens and 30,000 output tokens. The cost is \( (100{,}000 \times 3 + 30{,}000 \times 15) / 10^{6} = 0.75 \) dollars. A model priced at five times those rates costs 3.75 dollars for the same job. Neither figure is a concern for a single run, but a development loop of 20 prompt revisions over the same 200 abstracts multiplies the cost by 20, and a pipeline that feeds a long document into every call multiplies the input tokens by the document length.

Latency and rate limits determine wall-clock time. If each request takes 4 seconds and you send them one after another, 200 requests take 800 seconds, about 13 minutes. Sending ten at a time cuts that to around 80 seconds, unless the provider caps you at 50 requests per minute (an illustrative limit), in which case the job takes 4 minutes whatever you do. When a limit is exceeded the API returns an error, and a script that does not wait and retry will fail partway through, leaving a half-processed set of results. Always write batch scripts so that they log which inputs completed and can resume.

Price the Whole Loop, Not One Call

Before you run a batch, run five items and read the usage counts the API returns. Multiply by the number of items and by the number of revisions you expect to make. If the total surprises you, shorten the input or switch to a cheaper model for the development loop and use the better model only for the final run.

docs.title: Selecting a Model
docs.text:
Model selection is the choice of which model, through which access method, to use for a given task. It is a trade-off among capability, cost, latency, privacy, and reproducibility. There is no best model; there is a best model for a task under constraints. Two further distinctions shape the decision.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published, so that you can download and run them yourself, usually under a license that states what you may do with them. This is different from "open source" in the strict sense, because the training data and code may not be released. A local model is any model that runs on hardware you control, such as your laptop, a lab workstation, or a departmental cluster. Open-weight models are what make local models possible. Their appeal for research is concrete: your data never leaves your machine, the model works with no network connection, the exact weights can be archived with your results, and there is no per-token charge once the hardware exists. Their costs are equally concrete: capable models need substantial memory, usually a GPU, and the strongest hosted models are generally ahead of what you can run locally.

A related hazard is model version drift. Hosted models are updated, and a name such as a model family can point to different weights over time. The same prompt run six months apart can return different results, which silently invalidates a comparison. The defense is to record the exact model identifier, the date, and the settings with every result, to pin a dated version when the provider offers one, and to rerun a small fixed test set whenever the model changes. A local open-weight model has no drift unless you change the file, which is the reason it is attractive for work that must be reproduced years later.

Reading the scenario details is exploration and is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A local model is always the safest or cheapest choice. (2) The strongest hosted model is the right choice for every task. (3) A chat interface is adequate for any task because the model is the same.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluate-level work needs the learner to apply criteria to a case and defend a choice. Scenarios are written so that each path is correct for some cases, and so a single heuristic such as "always choose the best model" fails on at least two items.

Content:

Deciding factors: Privacy or data policy, Scale and automation, Reproducibility over time, Capability and effort.

  2. The learner chooses one of the three access paths and one of the four deciding factors and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether the path was correct and the "Why" sentence, then moves to the next scenario.
  4. After scenario 8 the sim shows the count correct, and for each missed scenario the misconception it exposes.

The correct path is always revealed after the single attempt. A final score "n of 8 correct" is shown, with whether the mastery threshold of 6 was met.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that local open-weight models fit data that cannot leave the site, offline work, and reproducibility, that hosted APIs fit scripted batches, and that a chat interface fits one-off exploration. The chapter's worked cost example is 200 abstracts costing 0.75 dollars at the stated illustrative prices.

docs.title: Adding Your Own Documents: Embeddings, Vector Search, and Retrieval
docs.text:
A model does not know your lab's notebook, your private papers, or last month's preprints. The usual remedy is not to retrain the model but to retrieve the relevant passages and place them in the prompt. Three concepts make this work, and they are best taken in order.

An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a piece of text, produced by a model trained so that texts with similar meaning receive vectors that point in similar directions. A real embedding has hundreds to thousands of numbers. Two sentences that share no words, such as "calibrating comparator offset" and "removing input-referred bias in a latch", can still land close together, because the vectors encode meaning and not spelling.

Vector search is the retrieval of the stored vectors most similar to the vector of a query. The common similarity measure is cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between two vectors. For vectors \( \mathbf{a} \) and \( \mathbf{b} \),

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{\lVert \mathbf{a} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{b} \rVert}. \]

A value near 1 means the vectors point in nearly the same direction, a value near 0 means they are unrelated, and a negative value means they point apart. Notice that the search always returns something: the top results are simply the least bad, and a weak match comes back with the same confident formatting as a strong one. A similarity threshold, below which results are discarded, is the guard against that.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines these steps. Your documents are split into passages and embedded once. At question time the question is embedded, the most similar passages are retrieved by vector search, and they are inserted into the prompt with an instruction to answer from them. The model's answer is then grounded in text you can point to, and the passages give you something to cite.

A small worked example uses two-dimensional toy vectors so that the geometry can be seen. The vectors are invented for illustration. Take a query vector \( q = (0.90, 0.25) \) and two stored passages \( d_1 = (0.95, 0.20) \) and \( d_3 = (0.15, 0.95) \). The cosine of \( q \) with \( d_1 \) is \( (0.90 \times 0.95 + 0.25 \times 0.20) / (0.934 \times 0.971) = 0.998 \). The cosine with \( d_3 \) is \( (0.90 \times 0.15 + 0.25 \times 0.95) / (0.934 \times 0.962) = 0.415 \). The first passage is retrieved, and the second is not.

Retrieved Does Not Mean Relevant

A common trap is to treat the passages a retrieval step returns as evidence that your documents contain the answer. The search ranks; it does not judge. Set a similarity threshold, instruct the model to answer "not found in the provided documents" when the passages do not contain the answer, and read the retrieved passages yourself on a sample.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
Everything so far has concerned the model and how to reach it. Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the prompt so that a model reliably produces the output you need. The word "engineering" is deliberate. A prompt is a specification, the model is a component with variable behavior, and the work is to write a specification precise enough that you can tell whether the component met it. It is not a bag of magic phrases, and phrases that work on one model version often fail on another.

A useful discipline is to treat a prompt as having four parts that can be named and inspected separately: the task (what to do), the constraints (the limits on how), the output format (the shape of the result), and the context (the material to work on). The techniques in this chapter correspond to these parts, plus two refinements, a role and examples.

docs.title: Clear Instructions
docs.text:
Clear instructions state one task, in terms of an observable outcome, using the vocabulary of the field. Three habits produce most of the gain. Use a verb that names the action ("list", "classify", "extract", "compare", "derive") instead of an open one ("look at", "think about", "help with"). State the goal and the audience, because the same material is summarized differently for a reading group and for a funding panel. And give one task per prompt where you can, because a prompt asking for five things gets five uneven answers.

The most reliable test of an instruction is to hand it to a competent colleague who has not seen the project and ask what they would produce. If two colleagues would produce visibly different outputs, the instruction underdetermines the task, and a model will resolve that ambiguity in whatever way its training data makes likely, not the way you intended.

A worked example shows the effect. The weak prompt is "Summarize this paper." The gaps are the length, the audience, the content to prioritize, and what to do when the paper does not state something. A model must guess all four. The revised prompt below says them explicitly. Read it first as plain text, then notice which sentence carries which of the four parts.

You are reviewing a paper for a graduate reading group in analog circuit design.

Summarize the attached paper's contribution in at most 120 words.
Use only information that appears in the attached text. If a value is not stated,
write "not stated" instead of estimating it.

After the summary, output a table with these columns:
Architecture | Process node | Supply voltage | Sampling rate | ENOB | Power
One row for the paper's main design. Example row (illustrative):
SAR | 65 nm | 1.0 V | 1 MS/s | 9.2 | 45 µW

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints are explicit limits on what the model may do or use: its length, its sources, its scope, and what it must not do. They matter more than they appear to, because without them the model fills every unspecified dimension with its defaults, and the defaults are tuned for a generic reader. The constraints that most often matter in research work fall into four families.

  • Source constraints limit what may be used: "use only the attached text", "cite only papers from the provided list".
  • Scope constraints limit the territory: "consider only successive-approximation converters, not pipeline architectures".
  • Length and style constraints limit the shape: "at most 120 words", "no marketing language".
  • Escape constraints give the model a sanctioned way out: "if the text does not state it, write 'not stated'".

The last family is the one most often missed, and it is the cheapest defense against hallucination. A model that is required to answer and is given no permitted way to say "unknown" will produce a plausible answer. Make "unknown" a legal output, and then look for how often it occurs.

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
An output format is an explicit statement of the shape of the response: a table with named columns, a JSON object with named fields, a numbered list, a fixed number of sentences. Its value is practical. A response in a known shape can be parsed by a script, compared across runs, and checked at a glance. For work that feeds a pipeline, ask for a machine-readable format, give the field names, and say what to do with missing values. For work that a human will read, a table with named columns serves nearly as well and is easier to scan.

A sample specification for a parseable result, with the purpose of each key explained first. The claim key holds one sentence from the paper, supported holds true or false, and evidence holds the supporting quotation or the string "not stated".

{
  "claim": "string, one sentence from the paper",
  "supported": "true or false",
  "evidence": "string, a quotation from the paper, or \"not stated\""
}

A Prompt Is a Specification You Can Test

Notice what the format buys you beyond tidiness. Once the answer has a named structure, "is this output valid?" becomes a question a script can answer, and verification stops depending on your attention.

docs.title: Role Prompting
docs.text: Role prompting assigns the model a role, such as "a reviewer for a circuits conference" or "a careful numerical analyst", at the start of the prompt. It works by shifting the style, vocabulary, and the set of considerations the model brings, and it is most useful for tone and perspective. It is weaker than it sounds as a way to add knowledge or accuracy: telling a model it is a world expert does not give it expertise it lacks. Use a role to set the viewpoint, and use constraints and examples to enforce the behavior.

docs.title: Few-Shot Examples
docs.text:
Few-shot examples are one or more worked input-and-output pairs placed in the prompt to show the model what you want. A prompt with no examples is called zero-shot. Examples are the strongest single way to communicate a format or a judgment that is hard to describe, such as how to label a borderline abstract. They have two costs: they consume context, and the model will imitate them closely, including their quirks. Choose examples that cover the range of cases, include a boundary case, and vary them so that a surface feature, such as always the same length, is not mistaken for the rule. Mark any invented example as illustrative so a reader does not take it for data.

Technique What it controls Typical failure if omitted Cost Clear instructions The task and audience Plausible answer to a different question Low Constraints Sources, scope, length, "unknown" Invented details; scope creep Low Output format Shape of the result Unparseable or inconsistent results Low Role prompting Tone and perspective Generic voice Very low Few-shot examples Format and judgment Inconsistent labels Context tokens

Table 2. The five prompt techniques of this chapter and what each controls.

The last MicroSim practices recognizing which technique a sentence of a prompt is carrying. This is a real skill: when a prompt misbehaves, the way to fix it is to find which component is missing or doing the wrong job.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the assembled prompt with sentence 1 highlighted.
  2. The learner chooses one of the five labels for the highlighted sentence and submits.
  3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the "Why" sentence, then highlights the next sentence.
  4. After sentence 10, the sim shows the count correct, and a tally of how many sentences carry each component. The learner should notice that constraints are the most numerous.

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked prompt contains a role, a length constraint of at most 120 words, a source constraint, an escape constraint, a table output format with six named columns, and one illustrative example row. The chapter states that role prompting sets viewpoint and does not add knowledge.

Your First Prompts Will Be Vague

If your early prompts get plausible but unusable answers, that is normal, because you know the context so well that it feels obvious. You have written methods sections for readers who lack your context. Write the prompt the same way, then change one thing at a time and keep the version that passes your check.

A final point connects this chapter to the next. Prompt engineering at this level is a way of writing a good single message. Real research tasks depend on more than one message: which documents to include, how to carry earlier results forward, how to test a prompt, and how to defend against hostile text. That wider view is context engineering, the subject of Chapter 4.

docs.title: Summary and Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Choosing a model is a constrained trade-off, and writing a prompt is writing a specification. Both are decisions you can make deliberately, record, and revisit, which is what turns casual use into research practice.

The main points to carry forward:

  • API access makes model use repeatable and scriptable, and API keys are secrets.
  • Token cost, latency, and rate limits decide whether a batch is practical. Price the whole loop, not one call.
  • Model selection weighs capability, cost, privacy, and reproducibility. A local open-weight model is the answer when data must stay on site, work is offline, or results must be rerun years later.
  • Model version drift silently changes hosted-model results, so record the model identifier, date, and settings.
  • Embeddings, vector search, and RAG bring your own documents into the prompt, and retrieval returns results whether or not they are relevant.
  • Clear instructions name one observable task for a stated audience.
  • Constraints bound sources, scope, and length, and an "unknown" escape is the cheapest guard against invention.
  • Output formats make results parseable and checkable.
  • Roles set viewpoint, and few-shot examples communicate format and judgment, at the cost of context.

You Can Pick and Specify

You can now choose among a chat interface, a hosted API, and a local open-weight model for a stated scenario, estimate what a batch will cost, and write a prompt with a clear task, explicit constraints, and a defined output format.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter moves from single prompts to managing everything a model sees. It covers selecting and compressing context, grounding answers in sources, handling long documents, testing prompts, and defending against prompt injection. It builds to multi-step and chained prompts for larger research tasks. After this chapter you can design and test a prompt workflow with acceptance criteria.
